messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Aroha's Reckoning

Aroha Ngata was sixty-seven years old when she first came to therapy, though she moved through the world as though she were carrying the weight of someone much older. She had worked as a database administrator for a mid-sized insurance firm in Sacramento for nearly thirty years—a job that suited her methodical mind, one where data followed rules and patterns and did not surprise you if you paid attention. But in the past eighteen months, even that refuge had begun to fracture.

The violence had come without warning, though Aroha would later understand that she had simply not been reading the signs. Robert had seemed gentle when they met at a community centre event three years ago, a widower like herself, with soft eyes and a way of listening that made her feel seen for the first time since her husband died. They had married after eighteen months of courtship. For the first six months of marriage, Aroha had felt almost reborn—someone had chosen her again, had wanted her in his life. She had not realized how much she had been waiting to feel that way.

The first time Robert hit her, it was because she had spoken out of turn at a dinner party, correcting something he had said about computers. He had driven her home in silence, and once inside, his hand had connected with the side of her face with such force that she fell against the kitchen counter. She remembered the shock more than the pain—the sense that the world had tilted on its axis. He had cried afterward, held her, apologized with a desperation that made her believe it would not happen again. But it did. Over the course of eight months, it happened seventeen times. Sometimes it was a shove when she moved too slowly. Sometimes it was his hand around her throat. Once, he had thrown a plate that caught her shoulder. Each time, the apologies came. Each time, Aroha found herself wondering what she had done to provoke him, what she had said wrong.

When she finally left him—after he had pinned her against a wall and told her she was worthless, that no one would ever want her—she had called her daughter in Auckland. Within two days, she was on a plane, and Robert was arrested. The legal proceedings took four months. He pleaded guilty to assault. He was sentenced to eighteen months in prison. By then, Aroha was back in Sacramento, back at her job, trying to convince herself that she could simply resume her life.

But the woman who returned to her apartment was not the woman who had left it. She had come to believe that her reactions since the event—the panic, the shame, the way she flinched at sudden movements—showed that she was a lousy coper, someone fundamentally unable to manage her own life. She had let a man fool her. She had stayed far longer than she should have. She had not seen what was obvious to everyone else. There was something wrong with her as a person, something that had drawn his violence toward her, some defect that made her unable to protect herself. These thoughts had become as familiar as her own breath.

At work, Aroha sat in her cubicle and avoided eye contact with her colleagues. When her supervisor, Marcus, tried to check in with her about a project, she looked past his shoulder at the wall behind him, unable to meet his gaze. She was certain that if he looked directly into her eyes, he would see the truth of her—the weakness, the poor judgment, the fundamental brokenness. She had taken to staying up until one or two in the morning, sitting in her living room with all the lights on, her body too wired with vigilance to surrender to sleep. When sleep finally came, it was fitful and full of dreams in which Robert's hands were around her throat and she could not scream.

The avoidance of touch had developed gradually. Her daughter had tried to hug her when she arrived in Auckland, and Aroha had stiffened, unable to bear the weight of another person's body against her own. Now, six months after leaving Robert, she crossed the street to avoid brushing past strangers on the sidewalk. When her colleague Janet had reached out to pat her arm in sympathy—someone must have told her something—Aroha had jerked away so sharply that Janet had looked wounded. She had not tried again.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she seek help. He had noticed that her work had become scattered, that she was making errors in datasets that had always been her strength, that she seemed to be disappearing into herself. He had asked her directly, in his office, if something was wrong. She had looked at her hands and told him she had been in an abusive relationship. He had listened without judgment and given her the name of a therapist. Aroha had called that evening, during the hours when she was awake anyway, too afraid to sleep, too ashamed to reach out during normal business hours.

What frightened her most was the possibility that she would never feel like herself again—that the woman she had been before Robert, the woman who had raised two children and managed complex databases and believed she was capable—was gone forever. What she was hoping for, though she barely dared to name it, was the chance to discover who she was now, in this new and terrifying version of her life.
